text: A network learns by adjusting its weights to make its error, which we call the loss, a little smaller. For that it needs to know, for every weight, which way to move it and how strongly the loss responds. Nudging one weight at a time and rerunning the network would take billions of forward passes for a model with billions of weights. Backpropagation gets every one of those answers from a single backward pass through the graph.

The quantity we want for each weight is a derivative, and it is best thought of as a sensitivity, like the ratio of a pair of gears. If turning one gear by a tiny amount turns the next by three times as much, the ratio is three. The derivative of the loss with respect to a weight is exactly that ratio: how much the loss moves for a tiny turn of that weight, with its sign telling us whether the loss goes up or down.

Each node in the graph only needs to know its own small gear ratios, which we call local derivatives. For addition they are simple: if you nudge either input of a sum, the output moves by exactly the same amount, so both local derivatives are one. For multiplication there is a pleasant swap. Nudge a in a times b and the product moves by b times as much, while nudging b moves it by a times as much.

Gears chain together, and so do derivatives. If the loss moves two units for every unit of c, and c moves three units for every unit of a, then the loss moves six units for every unit of a. This is the chain rule: to find how the loss depends on something far back in the graph, multiply the local ratios along the path that connects them.

Let us run it on the graph from the last lesson, where a times b, plus c, multiplied by f, gave minus eight, and treat that output as our loss. We start at the output, whose derivative with respect to itself is one. The last node multiplied d, which was four, by f, which was minus two, so by the swap rule the gradient flowing to f is four, and the gradient flowing to d is minus two.

Next comes the addition node that produced d. Addition passes its incoming gradient through unchanged, so c receives minus two, and so does the product of a and b. Finally the multiplication node applies the swap again: a receives minus two times b, which is six, and b receives minus two times a, which is minus four. Each number tells us how strongly the loss responds to a nudge in that value.

One more rule completes the picture. When a value is used in two places, its influence reaches the loss along two separate paths, and the total effect is the sum of the two. So a node collects gradients from every place it was used and adds them together. Overwriting a gradient instead of adding to it is the most common bug in hand-written backpropagation.

The order of the backward pass matters as well. A node can only pass its gradient on once it has received the contributions from everything that used it, so we visit the nodes in the reverse of the order in which the forward pass created them. Each edge is then handled exactly once, which is why the backward pass costs only a small multiple of the forward pass, however many weights there are.

With every gradient in hand, learning is a small step downhill. Since the gradient of a is six, increasing a would raise the loss, so we move a slightly in the opposite direction, and we do the same for every weight at once, subtracting a small multiple of its gradient. Repeat this many times and the loss falls, and that loop is the subject of the module on training.

Training a language model is this same procedure at enormous scale: one loss for how well it predicted the next tokens, one backward pass, and a gradient for every one of its billions of parameters. The method was made famous in 1986 by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, and when you call loss dot backward in PyTorch, this is what runs. Next we see what happens to these gradients in very deep networks, and why they can vanish.
